title: Father, forgive them
hook: from the cross: they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man forgiven everything who seized someone over a small debt. Your line was I was forgiven too. Which mercy did you remember? Today, forgiveness spoken at the worst possible moment. Day nine hundred fifty.

Luke's Gospel slows down at the place called Calvary. Two criminals, one on each side. A crowd standing and watching. And in that moment, before the soldiers cast lots for his clothes and the mocking that follows, Luke records a sentence from Jesus. It isn't a cry of pain. It isn't a curse. It's addressed upward, and it's about the people right in front of him. Today: Father, forgive them.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE ON EACH SIDE.` → `A SENTENCE ADDRESSED UPWARD.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In the King James: "Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the first word. Father. It's the same word that opens the prayer Jesus teaches in Luke, and he says it here, too, of all places. Not judge, not avenger. The family word, spoken from the worst day. Second, who he forgives. The sentence doesn't name names, and Christians have read it in different ways. Some hear it about the soldiers carrying out orders. Some widen it to everyone who had a hand in it. Others widen it further still, to every person, themselves included. The text leaves the circle open, and that openness is part of its force. Third, the reason he gives. For they know not what they do. That's a striking thing to say about people carrying out a crucifixion. Some readers point out that they know what their hands are doing; what they don't see, in this reading, is what it means: who this is, what it costs, what they've become part of. Read that way, the line holds two truths at once. A wrong is happening. And the people doing it don't fully understand it. Forgiveness here doesn't pretend the first truth away. It leans on the second. Fourth, what this does for ordinary life. Sometimes the people who hurt us aren't villains with a plan. They're tired, scared, careless, following orders, repeating what was done to them. They know what they did. They may not see all of what it did. That gap, the space between the act and the understanding, is where this sentence plants itself. It doesn't make the wrong smaller. It makes room for the person.
screen: `FATHER: THE FIRST WORD.` · `THE CIRCLE LEFT OPEN.` · `THEY KNOW WHAT, NOT WHAT IT MEANS.` · `ROOM FOR THE PERSON.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle low. Let one person who wronged you come into view. Not to relive it. Just enough to see their face. Then ask a quiet question: what didn't they understand? Maybe what it would cost you. Maybe what was happening in them at the time. Maybe something they still can't see. You don't have to excuse them. Simply wish them one thing: understanding. That someday they see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer with the line from Luke. The bell holds the time.
Father. The first word of Jesus's prayer from the cross in Luke, forgiving the people who didn't know what they were doing. Today's word.
Your line: they know not. Today, when someone hurts or annoys you, ask what they might not see, before you decide what they meant. Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Christians remember this line among the sayings of Jesus from the cross, read especially on Good Friday, and some churches meditate on the sayings one by one that day.

fork.setup: you're at Calvary, among the watching crowd. what does Luke record Jesus saying first?
options: a warning of judgment on them.
a prayer that they be forgiven.
fork.reveal: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." a prayer, addressed upward, for the people in front of him.

original.note: Greek, Luke 23:34: Father, the word Jesus begins with.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about forgiving people.
what it means: forgiveness spoken in the middle of the wrong, for people who, the line says, know not what they do.
what a scholar hears: the line opens with Father, the same word that opens the prayer Jesus teaches his followers in Luke 11.

sources.quoted: Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.

notes: Manuscript note deliberately left out of the voice: some early manuscripts of Luke lack 23:34a. A Keeper should decide whether to mention it.
'Others widen it further still' is a 'many' claim; consider 'Some Christians' under the claims rule.
Trapdoor floor 3 ties Luke 23:34 to Luke 11:2 ('Father'); the saying appears only in Luke, which the voice does not claim.
Myth item 3 relies on the order of Luke 23:34 (prayer, then parting garments).
howItsDone: Good Friday meditations on the sayings from the cross (the 'Seven Last Words') are a practice in some churches; no count given.

Editor pass: 'nails' and 'close enough to touch' cut (not in Luke 23); 'dice' made 'cast lots'; the 'they know what their hands are doing' reading attributed to some readers; myth item 2, which called the text's own words false, replaced; fork and trapdoor adjusted; practice opener varied.
Audit (2026-10-01): hook screen head 'the men doing the work' (not in the voice) replaced with the two criminals the voice names; myth item 'dice' made 'lots' to match Luke 23:34 KJV.
